title: The Didache
hookLine: an early manual: two ways, baptism in running water, fasting on Wednesdays and Fridays

lines: A HANDBOOK FOR A NEW CHURCH.
cards: A brand-new church needs a handbook. What goes in it? How to live.
How to baptize. When to fast, and how often to pray. What to do about a traveling preacher who shows up and won't leave.

An early Christian handbook covers all of it in a few short pages. On that last problem it's wonderfully practical: let the visiting apostle stay a day, two if he needs it. If he stays three, he's a false prophet.
If he asks for money, same verdict. Its name is the Didache.

teach.b: Didache is Greek for teaching. The book isn't in the Bible, but it gives a close look at how some early Christians lived. First, a fork in the road.
In Lightfoot's translation: "There are two ways, one of life and one of death, and there is a great difference between the two ways."
The way of life: love the God who made you, love your neighbor as yourself, and don't do to another what you wouldn't want done to you. That's the again in today's line, because the picture is older.

In Deuteronomy, Moses sets life and death before the people and says, in the Douay-Rheims, "Choose therefore life." Jesus speaks of a narrow gate and a wide one. The Didache hands the same choice to a new community.
Second, baptism: in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, in running water, living water. If there isn't any, use other water, cold if you can, warm if you must.
If there's not enough for that, pour water on the head three times, in that same threefold name. Strict about the meaning, generous about the river. Third, fasting and prayer.
Christians fast on Wednesday and Friday, it says, and pray the Lord's Prayer three times a day. Catholics still keep Friday as a day of penance. Fourth, the bread.

The Didache gives thanksgiving prayers for the cup and the broken bread, and one pictures the bread as grain once scattered over the mountains and gathered into one loaf, the way the Church is gathered from the ends of the earth.
A handbook about water, food and visitors, and underneath it all, two roads and a choice made again every day.

how: Catholics today keep Friday as a day of penance, some fast or abstain in small ways during the week, and the Didache is read by students of the early Church as a window into its first practices.

games.q: inside the Didache — tap the pairs.
p: one of life, one of death

s: the Didache says baptism must be in running water or not at all
running water first, then other water, then pouring on the head three times.
the Didache asks Christians to pray the Lord's Prayer three times a day
it names the prayer and the three times.
a visiting apostle may stay as long as he likes
a day, two if needed. three days and he's a false prophet.

games.q: you're preparing a baptism in a dry village. there's no river and no spring, only a little water in a jar. what do you do?
o: wait until you can reach a river.
pour water on the head three times.
games.why: the Didache says if there isn't enough water to baptize in, pour it on the head three times, in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

practice: If fasting is safe for you, choose one small thing to go without on Wednesday, the Didache's fast day: a snack, a second coffee, an hour of scrolling.
Decide now what that little hunger will remind you of: a person, a prayer, the two ways. If you pray, offer the day ahead.

wordCard.voice: Didache. Greek for teaching, and the name of an early Christian handbook: two ways, baptism, fasting and prayer. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: teaching — the short name of the early Christian handbook.

carryVoice: Your line: two ways, again. Moses, Jesus and the Didache all drew the same fork. Day seven hundred one.
